introduction: A website is eventually a running program on a machine. Before you can operate a cluster, you need to answer four smaller questions: which program is running, who owns it, where it listens, and what evidence explains its failure. This week makes those questions visible on your own Linux lab.

You will create a workspace, serve one harmless web page on your own computer, locate its process and socket, and recover a bad Git commit. Nothing here requires a cloud account. The tiny Python server is a learning instrument, not a production web server.

Work in two Ubuntu terminals. Terminal A keeps the server running; terminal B inspects it. Read each explanation before copying the command. Predict the result, compare the output, and write down one observation before continuing.
prerequisites: Complete the in-course lab setup using Ubuntu 24.04 LTS in WSL2 or a disposable VM.
Have Bash, Python 3, Git, curl, iproute2 and procps installed using the setup guide.
Use a new ~/dev-opps-lab folder for this course. If that name already contains unrelated work, choose a fresh folder and use it consistently.

concepts.title: A shell runs programs; a directory gives them context
paragraphs: The terminal is a window into a shell, the program that reads your command. A command has a program name followed by arguments. In `mkdir -p notes`, mkdir is the program, -p is an option, and notes is the directory name.

A relative path starts at your current directory. An absolute path starts at `/`. `~` expands to your user's home directory. Quoting a path keeps spaces inside one argument. When you see Permission denied, first inspect ownership and the path; adding sudo changes the authority of a command and can hide a wrong assumption.
concepts.example: From ~/dev-opps-lab, app/index.html names the file inside this lab. From another directory, the same text could name a different file.
concepts.judgment: Keep normal project work owned by your user. Use administrator authority only for the specific setup actions that require it.

concepts.title: A process and a listening socket are different evidence
paragraphs: A process is a running instance of a program. Linux assigns it a process ID, or PID, and a user identity. A socket is an endpoint for communication. A TCP listening socket has an address and port and waits for incoming connections.

127.0.0.1 is the loopback address: this machine talks to itself. Port 8000 is the numbered endpoint we choose for the exercise. A process can exist without opening that socket; a log can contain an old success message after the process has exited. Compare current process, socket and request evidence.
concepts.example: ps can show Python running while curl fails because Python is listening on port 8001 and the client asks for 8000.
concepts.judgment: Identify the owner before stopping a process. A command that kills every Python process can interrupt unrelated work.

concepts.title: Output, errors and exit status tell different parts of the story
paragraphs: Programs normally write ordinary output to standard output and diagnostics to standard error. Both appear in your terminal unless redirected. `>` writes standard output into a file, replacing that file. `2>` redirects standard error. A pipe `|` sends one program's standard output into another program.

Every completed command also supplies an exit status: zero conventionally means success, nonzero means failure. `$?` is the status of the immediately previous command, so save or print it before another command overwrites it. An HTTP error and a shell error are different: curl normally exits zero after receiving an HTTP 404 unless asked to fail on HTTP errors.
concepts.example: `python3 --version > notes/python-version.txt` records version output. It does not save unrelated future terminal output.
concepts.judgment: Record the command, its status, and relevant output together. A screenshot saying 'done' is weaker evidence than a reproducible observation.

concepts.title: Git records deliberate snapshots
paragraphs: Git's working tree is the files you edit. The staging area is the set of changes selected for the next snapshot. A commit records that snapshot with a parent and a message. A branch is a movable name for a line of commits.

A revert creates a new commit that undoes an earlier commit. The mistake remains visible in history, which is useful when explaining an incident to teammates. A branch does not create another copy of a running service; your process may continue using data it already loaded.
concepts.example: Commit A sets port 8000, B changes it to 8001, and C reverts B. The current file says 8000, and the history explains why.
concepts.judgment: Use a harmless lab configuration for this drill. Do not erase shared history to make an incident look as if it never happened.

steps.title: Create a workspace you can explain
steps.purpose: Run in terminal B. These directories separate application code, tests, notes and evidence. An empty directory is not tracked by Git until it contains a file.

commands.code:
mkdir -p ~/dev-opps-lab/{notes,app,tests,evidence}
cd ~/dev-opps-lab
pwd
ls -ld . notes app tests evidence
explain: mkdir creates directories; -p allows missing parent directories and already-existing directories. Bash brace expansion produces the four names before mkdir runs.
cd changes the current directory. pwd prints its absolute path.
ls lists entries; -l shows ownership and permissions; -d inspects the directories themselves rather than their contents.
commands.expected: The path ends in /dev-opps-lab. Four directories exist and are owned by your normal Linux user.
commands.troubleshoot: If a directory is owned by root, stop and inspect how it was created. Use a fresh user-owned lab folder rather than recursively changing unrelated files.

commands.code:
cat /etc/os-release > notes/environment.txt
free -h >> notes/environment.txt
python3 --version >> notes/environment.txt
git --version >> notes/environment.txt
cat notes/environment.txt
explain: cat prints the operating-system identification file; > creates or replaces this lab note.
free reports memory; -h uses readable units. >> appends instead of replacing previous observations.
python3 --version and git --version record the actual installed tools. The final cat displays the collected note.
commands.expected: A note containing Ubuntu version, memory totals, Python version and Git version.
commands.troubleshoot: If a command is missing, return to the setup guide. Available memory changes over time; a different value is not a failed lab.

steps.checkpoint: Explain the difference between > and >> before editing your evidence file.

steps.title: Create and serve a single page
steps.purpose: Start the server in terminal A. It serves only the designated web directory, which contains no private files.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab mkdir -p app/hello printf '%s\n' '

Dev Opps lab

' > app/hello/index.html python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory app/hello
explain: cd selects the lab; mkdir -p creates the dedicated public directory.
printf prints the quoted string followed by a newline; > writes it to index.html.
python3 -m runs Python's http.server module. 8000 chooses the TCP port. --bind restricts the listener to loopback. --directory restricts which directory is served.
The command stays in the foreground. Keep this terminal open; Ctrl+C will later interrupt this specific server.
commands.expected: Terminal A reports that it is serving on 127.0.0.1 port 8000 and waits for requests.
commands.troubleshoot: Address already in use means something already owns the endpoint. Use the next step to identify it; do not change firewall settings or kill an unknown process.

steps.checkpoint: The waiting terminal is the running service, not a frozen shell.

steps.title: Connect the request to its socket and owner
steps.purpose: Use terminal B while terminal A keeps running. Read the PID from ss; never copy a PID from someone else's screenshot.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/
ss -ltnp 'sport = :8000'
ps -u "$USER" -o pid,user,stat,%cpu,%mem,args
explain: curl sends a GET request. --fail makes HTTP status 400 or higher a command failure; --show-error keeps diagnostics visible.
ss shows sockets. -l selects listening sockets, -t TCP, -n numeric addresses/ports, and -p owning processes visible to your user. The quoted filter selects local port 8000.
ps lists processes; -u selects your user; -o selects PID, owner, state, CPU, memory and complete command. $USER expands your username; quotes keep it one argument.
commands.expected: curl prints the page. ss shows LISTEN on 127.0.0.1:8000 with a Python PID; the same PID appears in ps. Terminal A logs the GET request.
commands.troubleshoot: If ss shows a listener but curl returns the wrong page, compare its command and directory. If no listener exists, inspect terminal A's startup error.

commands.code:
ls -l app/hello/index.html
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/missing-page
printf 'curl exit status: %s\n' "$?"
explain: ls -l shows the file's owner and rwx permission bits: user, group, then others.
curl asks for a deliberately absent path; --fail turns its HTTP 404 into a nonzero exit.
printf immediately records $? before another command can replace it. Double quotes allow expansion of the saved shell status.
commands.expected: The missing page produces an HTTP 404 diagnostic and curl status 22. The server remains alive.
commands.troubleshoot: A connection error instead of 404 means you have not reached the server. Resolve the address/port/process issue before reasoning about paths.

steps.checkpoint: Describe one observation proving the process exists and another proving HTTP behavior.

steps.title: Commit a mistake, then preserve its recovery
steps.purpose: The port note is deliberately harmless configuration: it is not consumed by the running server. This isolates Git mechanics from service changes.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab
git init -b main
git config user.name 'Dev Opps Learner'
git config user.email 'learner@example.invalid'
printf 'PORT=8000\n' > app/lab.env
git add notes/environment.txt app/hello/index.html app/lab.env
git commit -m 'Record the first local service'
explain: git init -b main creates repository metadata with main as the initial branch; run this in the new course folder.

git config without --global sets a lab-only author identity. The example.invalid address is deliberately non-deliverable; replace it with a chosen public commit identity before sharing work if desired.
printf writes a non-secret configuration note. git add stages exactly the listed files; git commit records them with a message.
commands.expected: One initial commit exists, containing the environment note, page and port note.
commands.troubleshoot: If Git asks for identity, check you ran the local config in this repository. Do not add credentials or all home-directory files.

commands.code:
git switch -c practice/wrong-port || exit 1
printf 'PORT=8001\n' > app/lab.env
git diff
git add app/lab.env
git commit -m 'Practice an incorrect port note'
git revert --no-edit HEAD
cat app/lab.env
git log --oneline -3
git status --short
explain: git switch -c creates and switches to a practice branch.
printf changes one tracked file; git diff shows unstaged differences. git add selects that file and commit records the mistake.
git revert --no-edit HEAD creates a new inverse commit using the default message. HEAD means the current commit, which must be the deliberate mistake you just made.
cat verifies current content; log --oneline -3 shows three concise commits; status --short reveals remaining uncommitted changes.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
commands.expected: PORT=8000 is restored. History includes initial state, mistake and revert. Other files are unaffected.
commands.troubleshoot: If you made another commit before reverting, inspect git log and target the mistake's actual hash. Stop on conflicts and read the changed file; do not blindly reset the repository.

steps.checkpoint: Explain why the web server did not move to port 8001 when you edited this unused note.

failure.title: Two servers cannot own this same endpoint
failure.boundary: Only use the loopback server you started. Keep terminal A running. Terminal B's second server will fail before serving traffic.

inject.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab
python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory app/hello
printf 'second server exit status: %s\n' "$?"
explain: The command attempts to bind the same address and port as terminal A.
printf captures the failed startup's exit status immediately.
inject.expected: An Address already in use error and nonzero exit status.
inject.troubleshoot: If a second server starts, terminal A may have stopped or used a different address/port. Inspect both terminals.

explain: ss identifies the existing socket owner. ps connects that owner PID to a command.
curl proves the first service can still answer despite the second startup failing.
investigate.expected: One relevant listener remains, and the original page still responds.
investigate.troubleshoot: Read actual PIDs rather than assuming the newest Python process owns the socket.

hints: A startup failure in one process does not mean the already-running service failed.
Compare the bind address and port before changing either program.

explanation: The first process already owns the loopback TCP endpoint. The second exits during binding. The working response comes from the first process, so a working curl alone cannot prove your new deployment started.

explain: In terminal B, select unused port 8001 for a separate intentional service instance.
Keep it in the foreground; use terminal C for verification.
recover.expected: The second instance starts on port 8001.
recover.troubleshoot: If 8001 is occupied, inspect its owner. Do not displace someone else's process.

verification.code:
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8001/
ss -ltnp 'sport = :8000 or sport = :8001'
explain: Two requests exercise the two endpoints; ss shows their separate listening sockets and PIDs.
verification.expected: Both return the page, with distinct Python processes listening on distinct ports.
verification.troubleshoot: If only one works, inspect that terminal's startup and socket state.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish 'never started' from 'running on the wrong port'?
questions.hint: Use three observations rather than one log line.
questions.answer: A startup error plus no matching process supports never started. A matching process with a listener on another port supports wrong configuration. Inspect ps, ss and the current log, then request the observed endpoint. A PID alone does not prove readiness.

questions.prompt: Why did the 404 not stop the server?
questions.hint: The client's outcome and the service lifecycle are separate.
questions.answer: The server handled a request for an absent resource and returned an HTTP response. curl --fail reported that response as a client command failure. The server process continued accepting requests, which you can prove by requesting / afterward.

questions.prompt: What does a revert preserve that deleting the mistake from history would lose?
questions.hint: Think of a teammate investigating yesterday's incident.
questions.answer: It preserves the original change, its author and message, and a distinct recovery commit. Teammates can inspect what happened and why. Reverting source does not automatically restore a running process or external data.

exercise.brief: From a fresh terminal, produce a short incident note proving which process serves the page, what user owns it, and how you recovered the wrong port note.
constraints: Use only your loopback lab and normal user.
Do not delete Git history or stop unrelated processes.
deliverables: evidence/week-01.md with process/socket/request evidence, actual version information, three commit summaries and a five-minute explanation.
acceptance: A reader can reproduce the successful page request.
The socket PID matches the process owner and command.
The note distinguishes the deliberate second-server failure from an outage.
The current port note is 8000 and its mistake/revert remain visible.
hints: Record observations immediately after the command.
Explain why each observation matters, not only what it prints.
solution: Use pwd to establish context, ps and ss to connect process to socket, and curl to establish behavior.
Capture git log --oneline -3 and explain the inverse commit.
Write an alternative hypothesis and the observation that ruled it out.

cleanup.code:
printf '%s\n' 'In terminals A and B, press Ctrl+C once in each running server.'
ss -ltnp 'sport = :8000 or sport = :8001'
explain: printf displays the exact manual cleanup action. Ctrl+C interrupts the foreground server in that terminal; it does not target every Python process.
After stopping your instances, ss checks the two lab ports.
cleanup.expected: Your two server listeners disappear. Keep the workspace and Git history for next week.
cleanup.troubleshoot: If another listener remains, inspect its PID and owner before deciding whether it belongs to this lab.
